find: He stumbles in from the Moonraker's pub, hungover, and lectures his daughters on respectability while being unable to manage his own behaviour.
replace: He comes downstairs late from the house, lectures his daughters on respectability, then goes straight out to the Moonraker's. He cannot manage his own behaviour.
note: F30: the Act 1 stage direction has Hobson enter from the house on his way OUT to the Moonraker's; he does not stumble in from the pub.

find: the older, educated woman proposes to the timid, barely literate craftsman
replace: the educated woman proposes to the timid, barely literate craftsman
note: F31: Willie's stage direction says he is 'about thirty', the same age as Maggie, so he is not younger than her.

find: When Ada Figgins and her mother arrive to defend Ada's claim on Willie, the scene becomes a comic battle for possession of a man who barely speaks. Ada physically grabs Willie; Maggie calmly overrides them both.
replace: When Ada Figgins arrives with Willie's dinner and defends her claim on him, the scene becomes a comic battle for possession of a man who barely speaks. Ada takes his arm; Maggie calmly overrides them both. Ada's mother never appears on stage, though Willie admits he is afraid of her.
note: F22: Ada comes alone with Willie's dinner; Mrs Figgins is only spoken about.

find: But Maggie intercepts: she tells Willie that if Hobson strikes him, they will leave immediately.
replace: But Willie finds his voice: he warns that if Hobson touches him with the belt he will take Maggie and keep her, and that the two of them will set up on their own.
note: F23: the threat to leave is Willie's, not Maggie's; Maggie only says 'I'm watching you, my lad'.

find: By Act 2, he is beginning to change. Maggie insists that he learn to read and write — skills Hobson never bothered to teach him. Willie's education scenes are both comic and touching: he struggles with his letters but refuses to give up.
replace: By Act 2, he is beginning to change. Maggie then sets about his education: on their wedding night at the end of Act 3 she has him copying a writing exercise on a slate. Those scenes are both comic and touching, because he struggles with his letters but refuses to give up.
note: F19: the writing lessons are at the end of Act 3, not in Act 2.

find: By Act 2, he can declare with evident pride: "I've got my name wrote up on the windows" — a sign that he understands his new identity as a man of business, not just a cellar-worker.
replace: By Act 2, he can say: "I've got my name wrote up on the windows, but I dunno so much about being master." He has a new identity as a man of business, even if he is not yet sure of it.
note: F24: the full line is hedged, so the quotation does not show 'evident pride'.

find: The 1870 Education Act had introduced compulsory elementary education, but many working-class adults remained functionally illiterate. Willie's inability to read or write is a direct consequence of his class position — he was put to work as a child, not sent to school.
replace: The 1870 Education Act set up board schools to fill the gaps, but attendance only became compulsory under the 1880 Act, and many working-class adults stayed barely literate. Willie can read "a bit" and writes with difficulty, which is a direct result of his class position: he was put to work as a child instead of being sent to school.
note: F26 and F20: the 1870 Act did not make attendance compulsory (the 1880 Act did), and Willie is not wholly illiterate.

find: This linguistic arc is strong evidence for AO4 (writer's methods) — Brighouse uses Willie's changing speech patterns to dramatise his growing confidence and social mobility.

note: F3: AO4 on this section is spelling, punctuation and grammar; AO2 (methods) is not assessed here.

find: In Act 3, Hobson's drinking catches up with him in a scene that is both comic and symbolic. He falls through the cellar trapdoor of the Beenstock corn warehouse on Chapel Street while drunk, and finds himself facing a legal claim for trespass, damage to corn sacks, and spying on trade secrets.
replace: In Act 2, Hobson's drinking catches up with him in a way that is both comic and symbolic. He falls through the pavement cellar trap of the Beenstock corn warehouse on Chapel Street while drunk and sleeps there on the corn bags. The fall itself happens offstage: Fred Beenstock brings the news, and Maggie then has a claim drawn up for trespass, damage to the corn bags, and spying on trade secrets.
note: F15: the fall and the trespass claim belong to Act 2, and the fall is reported, not staged.

find: A doctor diagnoses Hobson with chronic alcoholism and warns that he must stop drinking or die.

find: The trespass case against Hobson becomes the mechanism for Maggie's return. Albert Prosser, now engaged to Alice, is the solicitor handling the case against Hobson. replace: The trespass case is Maggie's own device. She has Fred Beenstock and Albert Prosser, the solicitor courting Alice, draw it up, and Albert admits it is poor law that he would not want to take into court. Maggie never intends it to get there. At the wedding party in Act 3 she uses it to make Hobson settle out of court for five hundred pounds, which becomes two hundred and fifty each for Alice and Vickey: the marriage settlements he had refused to provide.
note: F17: the action is invented by Maggie and used in Act 3 to force the settlements; her return to Hobson's house is a separate event in Act 4.
